claim: MCL1 has critical antiapoptotic functions and its levels are tightly regulated by ubiquitylation and degradation.
source: MCL1 has critical antiapoptotic functions and its levels are tightly regulated by ubiquitylation and degradation, but mechanisms that drive this degradation, particularly in solid tumors, remain to be established.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about MCL1 function and regulation.

claim: Increased NOXA, mediated by kinase inhibitor activation of an integrated stress response, drives the degradation of MCL1 in prostate cancer cells.
source: We show here in prostate cancer cells that increased NOXA, mediated by kinase inhibitor activation of an integrated stress response, drives the degradation of MCL1
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: MARCH5 is the primary mediator of NOXA-dependent MCL1 degradation.
source: We show here in prostate cancer cells that increased NOXA, mediated by kinase inhibitor activation of an integrated stress response, drives the degradation of MCL1, and identify the mitochondria-associated ubiquitin ligase MARCH5 as the primary mediator of this NOXA-dependent MCL1 degradation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by multiple experiments including siRNA and CRISPR knockdown studies.

claim: Therapies that enhance MARCH5-mediated MCL1 degradation markedly enhance apoptosis in response to a BH3 mimetic agent targeting BCLXL.
source: Therapies that enhance MARCH5-mediated MCL1 degradation markedly enhance apoptosis in response to a BH3 mimetic agent targeting BCLXL, which may provide for a broadly effective therapy in solid tumors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding with therapeutic implications, supported by experimental data.

claim: Increased MCL1 in response to MARCH5 loss does not strongly sensitize to BH3 mimetic drugs targeting MCL1.
source: Conversely, increased MCL1 in response to MARCH5 loss does not strongly sensitize to BH3 mimetic drugs targeting MCL1, but instead also sensitizes to BCLXL inhibition
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing responses to MCL1 and BCLXL inhibitors.

claim: MARCH5 loss sensitizes cells to BCLXL inhibition despite increased MCL1.
source: Conversely, increased MCL1 in response to MARCH5 loss does not strongly sensitize to BH3 mimetic drugs targeting MCL1, but instead also sensitizes to BCLXL inhibition, revealing a codependence between MARCH5 and MCL1 that may also be exploited in tumors with MARCH5 genomic loss.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing apoptotic responses to ABT-263.

claim: There is a codependence between MARCH5 and MCL1.
source: Conversely, increased MCL1 in response to MARCH5 loss does not strongly sensitize to BH3 mimetic drugs targeting MCL1, but instead also sensitizes to BCLXL inhibition, revealing a codependence between MARCH5 and MCL1 that may also be exploited in tumors with MARCH5 genomic loss.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by CRISPR screen data showing co-dependency patterns.

claim: Androgen deprivation therapy is the standard treatment for metastatic prostate cancer.
source: Androgen deprivation therapy to suppress activity of the androgen receptor (AR) is the standard treatment for metastatic prostate cancer (PCa), but tumors invariably recur (castration-resistant prostate cancer, CRPC).
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Tumors treated with androgen deprivation therapy invariably recur as castration-resistant prostate cancer.
source: Androgen deprivation therapy to suppress activity of the androgen receptor (AR) is the standard treatment for metastatic prostate cancer (PCa), but tumors invariably recur (castration-resistant prostate cancer, CRPC).
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The majority of castration-resistant prostate cancers initially respond to agents that further suppress AR, but most men relapse within 1-2 years.
source: The majority will initially respond to agents that further suppress AR, but most men relapse within 1–2 years and these relapses appear to be driven by multiple AR dependent and independent mechanisms (Watson et al., 2015; Yuan et al., 2014), which may include increased expression of anti-apoptotic proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Relapses in castration-resistant prostate cancer appear to be driven by multiple AR dependent and independent mechanisms, which may include increased expression of anti-apoptotic proteins.
source: The majority will initially respond to agents that further suppress AR, but most men relapse within 1–2 years and these relapses appear to be driven by multiple AR dependent and independent mechanisms (Watson et al., 2015; Yuan et al., 2014), which may include increased expression of anti-apoptotic proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Anti-apoptotic BCL2 family proteins (including BCL2, BCLXL, and MCL1) act by neutralizing BAX and BAK, and by inhibiting the BH3-only pro-apoptotic proteins that can activate BAX/BAK.
source: The anti-apoptotic BCL2 family proteins (including BCL2, BCLXL, and MCL1) act by neutralizing BAX and BAK, and by inhibiting the BH3-only pro-apoptotic proteins that can activate BAX/BAK (primarily BIM) (Montero and Letai, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: BH3-mimetic drugs can enhance apoptosis by mimicking the activity of BH3-only pro-apoptotic proteins and thereby antagonizing the anti-apoptotic BCL2 family proteins.
source: These interactions are mediated by the BH3 domain, and BH3-mimetic drugs can enhance apoptosis by mimicking the activity of BH3-only pro-apoptotic proteins and thereby antagonizing the anti-apoptotic BCL2 family proteins (Merino et al., 2018; Knight et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: ABT-737 and ABT-263 are BH3-mimetics that directly bind to BCL2, BCLXL, and BCLW but not MCL1.
source: ABT-737 (Oltersdorf et al., 2005) and ABT-263 (navitoclax, orally bioavailable analogue of ABT-737) (Tse et al., 2008) are BH3-mimetics that directly bind to BCL2, BCLXL, and BCLW (but not MCL1), which blocks their binding to pro-apoptotic BH3 only proteins such as BIM and their ability to neutralize BAX/BAK.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Navitoclax has single-agent activity in hematological malignancies.
source: Navitoclax has single-agent activity in hematological malignancies (Roberts et al., 2012), but causes thrombocytopenia due to BCLXL inhibition.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Navitoclax causes thrombocytopenia due to BCLXL inhibition.
source: Navitoclax has single-agent activity in hematological malignancies (Roberts et al., 2012), but causes thrombocytopenia due to BCLXL inhibition.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: ABT-199 (venetoclax) is a BCL2-specific agent that spares platelets and is FDA approved for chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
source: A BCL2-specific agent that spares platelets (ABT-199, venetoclax) is similarly active and is now FDA approved for chronic lymphocytic leukemia (Pan et al., 2014; Roberts et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Most solid tumors are resistant to BCL2/BCLXL BH3 mimetics, which appears to reflect an important role for MCL1.
source: In contrast, most solid tumors are resistant to these agents (Faber et al., 2015), which appears to reflect an important role for MCL1 (Faber et al., 2015; van Delft et al., 2006; Konopleva et al., 2006; Santer et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2017; Xiao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Preclinical studies indicate that navitoclax may be efficacious in solid tumors when used in combination with other agents that decrease MCL1 expression.
source: Indeed, preclinical studies indicate that navitoclax may be efficacious in solid tumors when used in combination with other agents acting through a variety of mechanisms, including by decreasing MCL1 expression (Faber et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2015; Leverson et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2011; Modugno et al., 2015; Anderson et al., 2016; Tong et al., 2017; Arai et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: BH3 mimetics that target MCL1 (including AMG176, S63845 and AZD5991) are now becoming available and may have single agent activity in a subset of tumors.
source: BH3 mimetics that target MCL1 (including AMG176, S63845 and AZD5991) are now becoming available and may have single agent activity in a subset of tumors (Kotschy et al., 2016; Ashkenazi et al., 2017; Letai, 2016; Merino et al., 2017; Tron et al., 2018; Caenepeel et al., 2018), but efficacy in most solid tumors will likely still require combination therapies (Merino et al., 2018; Kotschy et al., 2016; Merino et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Efficacy of MCL1 antagonists in most solid tumors will likely still require combination therapies.
source: BH3 mimetics that target MCL1 (including AMG176, S63845 and AZD5991) are now becoming available and may have single agent activity in a subset of tumors (Kotschy et al., 2016; Ashkenazi et al., 2017; Letai, 2016; Merino et al., 2017; Tron et al., 2018; Caenepeel et al., 2018), but efficacy in most solid tumors will likely still require combination therapies (Merino et al., 2018; Kotschy et al., 2016; Merino et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Navitoclax in combination with several kinase inhibitors (erlotinib, lapatinib, cabozantinib, sorafenib) can induce rapid and marked apoptotic responses in PCa cells.
source: We reported previously that navitoclax (acting through BCLXL blockade), in combination with several kinase inhibitors (erlotinib, lapatinib, cabozantinib, sorafenib) could induce rapid and marked apoptotic responses in PCa cells (Arai et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding from the authors' prior work and supported by a citation.

claim: The apoptotic response to navitoclax and kinase inhibitors was preceded by a dramatic increase in MCL1 degradation.
source: This response was preceded by a dramatic increase in MCL1 degradation, and we confirmed that navitoclax could drive apoptotic responses in vitro and in vivo in PCa cell that were depleted of MCL1 by RNAi or CRISPR.
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding from the authors' prior work.

claim: The enhanced MCL1 degradation in response to kinase inhibitors was not mediated by GSK3β-mediated phosphorylation or by the ubiquitin ligase HUWE1/MULE.
source: Significantly, the enhanced MCL1 degradation in response to kinase inhibitors was not mediated by well-established mechanisms including through GSK3β-mediated phosphorylation (and the downstream ubiquitin ligases βTrCP or Fbw7), or by the ubiquitin ligase HUWE1/MULE that has been reported to mediate both basal MCL1 degradation and MCL1 degradation in response to DNA damage and NOXA binding (Gomez-Bougie et al., 2011; Guikema et al., 2017; Zhong et al., 2005; Warr et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding from the authors' prior work and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Treatment with kinase inhibitors initiates an integrated stress response leading to increased ATF4 protein and subsequent increased transcription of NOXA.
source: In this study, we found that treatment with kinase inhibitors initiates an integrated stress response (ISR) leading to increased ATF4 protein and subsequent increased transcription of NOXA, and that the enhanced degradation of MCL1 was NOXA-dependent.
evidence: This is stated as a primary finding of the current study and supported by experimental data.

claim: MARCH5 is a RING-finger E3 ligase with an established function in mediating the ubiquitylation and degradation of several proteins that regulate mitochondrial fission and fusion.
source: MARCH5 is a RING-finger E3 ligase with an established function in mediating the ubiquitylation and degradation of several proteins that regulate mitochondrial fission and fusion (Chen et al., 2017; Park et al., 2014; Yonashiro et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2016; Cherok et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by multiple citations.

claim: MARCH5 depletion abrogated the decrease in MCL1 in response to cellular stress and substantially increased basal MCL1 in multiple epithelial cancer cell lines.
source: MARCH5 depletion both abrogated the decrease in MCL1 in response to cellular stress and substantially increased basal MCL1 in multiple epithelial cancer cell lines, indicating that MARCH5 makes a major contribution to regulating MCL1 levels under basal conditions and in responses to cellular stress.
evidence: This is stated as a primary finding and supported by experimental data showing effects of MARCH5 depletion.

claim: MARCH5 makes a major contribution to regulating MCL1 levels under basal conditions and in responses to cellular stress.
source: MARCH5 depletion both abrogated the decrease in MCL1 in response to cellular stress and substantially increased basal MCL1 in multiple epithelial cancer cell lines, indicating that MARCH5 makes a major contribution to regulating MCL1 levels under basal conditions and in responses to cellular stress.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: MARCH5 genomic loss occurs in approximately 5% of prostate cancer.
source: Conversely, increased MCL1 in response to MARCH5 loss does not strongly sensitize to BH3 mimetic drugs targeting MCL1, but instead also sensitizes to BCLXL inhibition, revealing a codependence between MARCH5 and MCL1 that may also be exploited in tumors with MARCH5 genomic loss.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by genomic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Erlotinib treatment for 4 hours can rapidly and markedly enhance the proteasome-dependent degradation of MCL1.
source: As we reported previously, multiple kinase inhibitors including the EGFR inhibitor erlotinib could rapidly (within 4 hr) and markedly enhance the proteasome-dependent degradation of MCL1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Erlotinib treatment for 4 hours did not decrease BIM in LNCaP cells.
source: Consistent with our previous results, 4 hr treatment with erlotinib did not decrease BIM, indicating that loss of BIM is not a basis for the marked decrease in MCL1 protein (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1A.

claim: NOXA expression was increased by erlotinib treatment.
source: In contrast, NOXA expression was increased by erlotinib, suggesting this may drive the increased MCL1 degradation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1A.

claim: Depleting NOXA with siRNA suppressed the erlotinib-mediated decrease in MCL1.
source: Indeed, depleting NOXA with three different siRNA suppressed this decrease in MCL1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1B.

claim: More complete depletion of NOXA with pooled siRNAs prevented the erlotinib-mediated MCL1 reduction.
source: Moreover, more complete depletion of NOXA with the pooled siRNAs prevented the erlotinib-mediated MCL1 reduction, indicating a NOXA-dependent mechanism for decreasing MCL1 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1C.

claim: Depletion of BIM by siRNA caused a decrease in basal MCL1 but did not prevent the further decrease in MCL1 in response to erlotinib.
source: In contrast, while depletion of BIM by siRNA caused a decrease in basal MCL1, it did not prevent the further decrease in MCL1 in response to erlotinib (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1D.

claim: Erlotinib rapidly upregulated NOXA mRNA within 2 hours.
source: Erlotinib rapidly (within 2 hr) upregulated NOXA mRNA (Figure 1E), indicating a transcriptional mechanism for increasing NOXA protein.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 1E.

claim: Inhibiting new synthesis of mRNA with actinomycin D decreased basal NOXA protein and prevented the erlotinib-mediated upregulation of NOXA.
source: Consistent with this finding, inhibiting new synthesis of mRNA with actinomycin D decreased basal NOXA protein, and prevented the erlotinib-mediated upregulation of NOXA (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1F.

claim: Actinomycin D prevented the erlotinib-mediated MCL1 reduction.
source: Actinomycin D similarly decreased basal MCL1 protein expression through transcriptional repression, but importantly prevented the erlotinib-mediated MCL1 reduction (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1F.

claim: S63845 increased basal MCL1 expression and prevented the erlotinib-mediated decrease in MCL1.
source: Significantly, S63845 increased basal MCL1 expression and prevented the erlotinib-mediated decrease in MCL1 (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1G.

claim: Erlotinib induces transcriptional upregulation of NOXA, and this increase in NOXA is directly enhancing MCL1 degradation.
source: Together, these data show that erlotinib induces transcriptional upregulation of NOXA, and indicate that this increase in NOXA is directly enhancing MCL1 degradation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Treatment with erlotinib did not cause any change in p53 expression.
source: However, treatment with erlotinib did not cause any change in p53 expression (Figure 2A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), indicating a p53-independent mechanism for increasing NOXA mRNA.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Erlotinib rapidly increased phosphorylation of eIF2α within 30 minutes.
source: Consistent with ISR activation, we found that erlotinib rapidly (within 30 min) increased phosphorylation of eIF2α (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2B.

claim: Both PERK and GCN2 appear to be contributing to ISR activation by erlotinib.
source: Both PERK and GCN2 appear to be contributing to this ISR activation as MCL1 degradation in response to erlotinib was prevented by siRNA targeting PERK and GCN2 in combination, but not by either alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Phosphorylation of eIF2α in response to erlotinib was associated with an increase in ATF4 protein.
source: Indeed, eIF2α phosphorylation in response to erlotinib was associated with an increase in ATF4 protein (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2B.

claim: An increase in NOXA protein was observed after 60-90 minutes of erlotinib treatment, coinciding with the increase in ATF4 and decrease in MCL1.
source: Nonetheless, an increase in NOXA protein was observed after 60–90 min of erlotinib treatment, and this rapid time course coincided with the increase in ATF4 and decrease in MCL1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2B.

claim: ISRIB decreased basal ATF4 and suppressed the erlotinib-mediated increase in ATF4 and NOXA.
source: Moreover, treatment with an ISR inhibitor (ISRIB), which suppresses the effects of eIF2α phosphorylation (Sidrauski et al., 2013), decreased basal ATF4 and suppressed the erlotinib-mediated increase in ATF4 and NOXA, providing further evidence for this pathway (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2C and a citation.

claim: ISRIB suppressed the erlotinib-mediated increase in NOXA mRNA.
source: Consistent with these findings, ISRIB suppressed the erlotinib-mediated increase in NOXA mRNA (Figure 2D), while MCL1 mRNA was unaffected by these treatments (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2D.

claim: MCL1 mRNA was unaffected by erlotinib or ISRIB treatment.
source: Consistent with these findings, ISRIB suppressed the erlotinib-mediated increase in NOXA mRNA (Figure 2D), while MCL1 mRNA was unaffected by these treatments (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2E.

claim: Activation of the ISR by erlotinib drives the rapid induction of NOXA, which then promotes MCL1 degradation.
source: Together, these findings indicate that activation of the ISR by erlotinib drives the rapid induction of NOXA, which then promotes MCL1 degradation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: HUWE1 depletion does not prevent the erlotinib-mediated increase in NOXA or the subsequent decrease in MCL1.
source: Figure 3—figure supplement 1A shows that HUWE1 depletion does not affect the erlotinib-mediated increase in NOXA, and that it does not prevent the subsequent decrease in MCL1.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment with NEDD8 inhibitor MLN4924 increased p27 but did not increase MCL1 or block the effects of erlotinib.
source: Treatment with NEDD8 inhibitor MLN4924 increased p27 (a known target of cullin-dependent E3 ligase CUL4), but did not increase MCL1 or block the effects of erlotinib (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MLN4924 moderately decreased MCL1 protein, which may be due to an increase in NOXA.
source: Indeed, MLN4924 moderately decreased MCL1 protein, which may be due to an increase in NOXA, whose degradation is mediated by a cullin-dependent E3 ligase (Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the text as an interpretation of the data and supported by a citation.

claim: MLN4924 failed to prevent the decrease in MCL1 in response to lapatinib.
source: MLN4924 similarly failed to prevent the decrease in MCL1 in response to lapatinib (EGFR/ERBB2 inhibitor) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), indicating that a cullin-independent mechanism is driving the increased MCL1 degradation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A cullin-independent mechanism is driving the increased MCL1 degradation in response to kinase inhibitors.
source: MLN4924 similarly failed to prevent the decrease in MCL1 in response to lapatinib (EGFR/ERBB2 inhibitor) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), indicating that a cullin-independent mechanism is driving the increased MCL1 degradation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the MLN4924 experiments.

claim: PARKIN depletion increased its target protein p62 but did not increase MCL1 or block the effect of erlotinib.
source: However, while PARKIN depletion increased its target protein p62, it did not increase MCL1 or block the effect of erlotinib (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Depleting MARCH5 with siRNA increased basal expression of MCL1 and MiD49 in LNCaP cells.
source: Significantly, depleting MARCH5 with siRNA increased basal expression of MCL1 and a known MARCH5 substrate, MiD49, in LNCaP cells (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: MARCH5 depletion did not increase MCL1 mRNA.
source: MARCH5 depletion did not increase MCL1 mRNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), further supporting a posttranscriptional mechanism for increasing MCL1.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: MARCH5 depletion increased basal MCL1 in PC3 PCa cells and in additional prostate, breast and lung cancer cell lines.
source: MARCH5 depletion also increased basal MCL1 in PC3 PCa cells (Figure 3B) and in additional prostate, breast and lung cancer cell lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–L).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–L.

claim: MARCH5 is a major mediator of basal MCL1 degradation in epithelial cancer cell lines.
source: These results show that MARCH5 is a major mediator of basal MCL1 degradation in epithelial cancer cell lines.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the MARCH5 depletion experiments across multiple cell lines.

claim: MARCH5 depletion prevented the decrease in MCL1 by erlotinib and cabozantinib in LNCaP cells.
source: Significantly, MARCH5 depletion prevented the decrease in MCL1 by erlotinib and cabozantinib (C-MET/VEGFR2 inhibitor) in LNCaP cells (Figure 3A,B), and in other prostate cancer cells (PC3 and DU145 cells) (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1M), indicating that the decreases in MCL1 by these kinase inhibitors are mediated by MARCH5.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The decreases in MCL1 by erlotinib and cabozantinib are mediated by MARCH5.
source: Significantly, MARCH5 depletion prevented the decrease in MCL1 by erlotinib and cabozantinib (C-MET/VEGFR2 inhibitor) in LNCaP cells (Figure 3A,B), and in other prostate cancer cells (PC3 and DU145 cells) (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1M), indicating that the decreases in MCL1 by these kinase inhibitors are mediated by MARCH5.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the MARCH5 depletion experiments.

claim: MARCH5 depletion did not prevent MCL1 loss in cells treated with dinaciclib.
source: In contrast, MARCH5 depletion did not prevent MCL1 loss in cells treated with dinaciclib (Figure 3A), which decreases MCL1 mRNA through inhibition of CDK9 and subsequent decrease in MCL1 transcription.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3A.

claim: Dinaciclib decreases MCL1 mRNA through inhibition of CDK9 and subsequent decrease in MCL1 transcription.
source: In contrast, MARCH5 depletion did not prevent MCL1 loss in cells treated with dinaciclib (Figure 3A), which decreases MCL1 mRNA through inhibition of CDK9 and subsequent decrease in MCL1 transcription.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about dinaciclib's mechanism of action.

claim: CRISPR/CAS9 deletion of MARCH5 resulted in a marked increase of MCL1 expression and MiD49 in each of three MARCH5 depleted lines.
source: Consistent with the RNAi results, there was a marked increase of MCL1 expression, as well of the MARCH5 substrate MiD49, in each of three MARCH5 depleted lines (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3D.

claim: Erlotinib no longer decreased MCL1 in MARCH5 depleted lines generated by CRISPR.
source: Moreover, erlotinib no longer decreased MCL1 in these MARCH5 depleted lines (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3D.

claim: Transient overexpression of exogenous MARCH5 decreased MCL1 in control and MARCH5 depleted cells.
source: As expected, transient overexpression of exogenous MARCH5 decreased MCL1 in control and MARCH5 depleted cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3E.

claim: MARCH5 depletion by CRISPR or siRNA increased NOXA protein in LNCaP cells and in additional cell lines.
source: Interestingly, and consistent with a previous report (Subramanian et al., 2016), MARCH5 depletion by CRISPR or siRNA also increased NOXA protein in LNCaP cells (Figure 3D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, respectively), and in additional cell lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–L).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in multiple figures and a citation.

claim: MARCH5 depletion did not increase, but instead decreased NOXA mRNA.
source: MARCH5 depletion did not increase, but instead decreased NOXA mRNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), indicating this increase in NOXA protein is through a post-transcriptional mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The increase in NOXA protein after MARCH5 depletion is through a post-transcriptional mechanism.
source: MARCH5 depletion did not increase, but instead decreased NOXA mRNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), indicating this increase in NOXA protein is through a post-transcriptional mechanism.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the mRNA and protein data.

claim: MCL1 can protect NOXA from proteasome-mediated degradation.
source: One plausible mechanism is through increased binding to MCL1, as a previous study found that MCL1 could protect NOXA from proteasome-mediated degradation (Craxton et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a plausible mechanism and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The increased levels of NOXA and BIM in MARCH5 depleted cells coincided with increased binding of these proteins to MCL1.
source: Consistent with this mechanism, the increased levels of NOXA and of BIM in MARCH5 depleted cells coincided with increased binding of these proteins to MCL1 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3F.

claim: S63845 decreased both NOXA and BIM in MARCH5-depleted cells.
source: Significantly, S63845 decreased both NOXA and BIM in the MARCH5-depleted cells, consistent with them being stabilized by MCL1 (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3G.

claim: S63845 increased MCL1 in both the control and MARCH5 depleted cells.
source: Of note, S63845 increased MCL1 in both the control and MARCH5 depleted cells, indicating that additional ubiquitin ligases may partially compensate for MARCH5 loss in driving basal MCL1 degradation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3G.

claim: Cells with CRISPR-mediated MCL1 depletion had markedly reduced NOXA and BIM.
source: Cells with CRISPR-mediated MCL1 depletion had markedly reduced NOXA and BIM, providing further evidence that MCL1 protects both from degradation (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3H.

claim: NOXA and BIM were increased in cells that overexpress ectopic MCL1.
source: Conversely, NOXA and BIM were increased in cells that overexpress ectopic MCL1 (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3I.

claim: The increases in NOXA and BIM were greater in MARCH5-depleted cells compared to cells overexpressing ectopic MCL1, despite comparable MCL1 levels.
source: However, while MCL1 levels were comparable in cells overexpressing ectopic MCL1 and in MARCH5-depleted cells, the increases in NOXA and BIM were greater in the latter MARCH5-depleted cells.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an observation from comparing the data.

claim: MARCH5-mediated ubiquitylation of MCL1 in MCL1-NOXA complexes may drive degradation of the complex or be coupled to the degradation of NOXA mediated by a distinct ubiquitin ligase.
source: One explanation for this difference with respect to NOXA (and possibly BIM) is that the MARCH5-mediated ubiquitylation of MCL1 in MCL1-NOXA complexes may drive degradation of the complex, or be coupled to the degradation of NOXA mediated by a distinct ubiquitin ligase.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative explanation for the observed differences.

claim: Erlotinib treatment, in combination with proteasome inhibition, enhanced the interaction between MARCH5 and MCL1.
source: Consistent with this conclusion, we found by coimmunoprecipitation that erlotinib treatment, in combination with proteasome inhibition, enhanced the interaction between MARCH5 and MCL1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4A.

claim: Erlotinib did not alter MCL1 phosphorylation at sites that have been shown to enhance its ubiquitylation and degradation.
source: We have previously found that erlotinib did not alter MCL1 phosphorylation at sites that have been shown to enhance its ubiquitylation and degradation (Arai et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding from the authors' prior work and supported by a citation.

claim: Erlotinib treatment did not have any clear effects on the phosphorylation of MCL1, BIM, or NOXA in LNCaP cells cultured under standard conditions in medium with fetal bovine serum.
source: Erlotinib treatment did not have any clear effects on the phosphorylation of MCL1, BIM, or NOXA in LNCaP cells cultured under standard conditions in medium with fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by phospho-tag gel data in Figure 4B.

claim: EGF stimulation of growth-arrested LNCaP cells caused a dramatic increase in BIM phosphorylation.
source: As a positive control for detection of phosphorylation we growth arrested LNCaP cells by culturing in medium with charcoal stripped serum (CSS), which is depleted of steroids and growth factors. As expected, EGF stimulation of these cells caused a dramatic increase in BIM phosphorylation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by phospho-tag gel data in Figure 4B.

claim: Erlotinib treatment did not clearly enhance MCL1 binding of NOXA versus BIM in MARCH5 knockout cells.
source: Erlotinib treatment did not clearly enhance MCL1 binding of NOXA versus BIM (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4C.

claim: Treatment with erlotinib increased NOXA and decreased MCL1, but did not decrease other MARCH5 substrates (MiD49, MFN1, and FUNDC1).
source: Treatment with erlotinib again increased NOXA and decreased MCL1, but did not decrease other MARCH5 substrates (MiD49, MFN1, and FUNDC1) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 4D.

claim: MFN1 and FUNDC1 are not undergoing MARCH5-mediated degradation under basal conditions.
source: Interestingly, while MiD49 was increased in the MARCH5 knockout cells (see also Figure 3E and H), MFN1 and FUNDC1 were not altered, indicating that these latter substrates are not undergoing MARCH5-mediated degradation under basal conditions.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data comparing control and MARCH5 knockout cells.

claim: Erlotinib is not generally enhancing MARCH5 activity.
source: In any case, this result indicates that erlotinib is not generally enhancing MARCH5 activity.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the observation that erlotinib does not affect other MARCH5 substrates.

claim: Treatment with erlotinib for 2 hours did not change the mitochondrial localization of MARCH5.
source: Consistent with previous reports, cellular fractionation showed that MARCH5 was primarily located to mitochondria (Figure 4E). Treatment with erlotinib for 2 hr (prior to a substantial decrease in MCL1) did not change this localization of MARCH5.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cellular fractionation data in Figure 4E.

claim: Erlotinib did not increase the mitochondrial localization of MCL1, BIM or NOXA.
source: Moreover, it did not increase the mitochondrial localization of MCL1, BIM or NOXA, indicating that erlotinib-mediated MCL1 degradation is not through increased targeting of these latter proteins to mitochondria.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cellular fractionation data in Figure 4E.

claim: MARCH5 depletion did not clearly alter the fraction of MCL1 associated with mitochondria.
source: Finally, MARCH5 depletion did not clearly alter the fraction of MCL1 associated with mitochondria.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an observation from the cellular fractionation experiments.

claim: Treatment with erlotinib or lapatinib for 4 hours decreased MCL1 in C4-2 cells.
source: Similar to LNCaP cells, treatment with erlotinib or lapatinib for 4 hr under conditions used for the Seahorse assays decreased MCL1 in C4-2 cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 4F.

claim: Neither erlotinib nor lapatinib changed maximal oxygen consumption rate in C4-2 cells.
source: We then treated with erlotinib or lapatinib for 2 hr and assessed oxygen consumption. Neither erlotinib nor lapatinib changed maximal oxygen consumption rate (Figure 4G,H), suggesting that EGFR inhibition is not promoting functional damage to mitochondrial regarding ATP production.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Seahorse data in Figure 4G,H.

claim: Erlotinib and lapatinib increased basal oxygen consumption (ATP linked respiration) in C4-2 cells.
source: Intriguingly, erlotinib and lapatinib increased basal oxygen consumption (ATP linked respiration) (Figure 4G,I), indicating a shift from fermentation to increased oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Seahorse data in Figure 4G,I.

claim: MARCH5 is not altered in response to erlotinib, and its increased degradation of MCL1 is driven primarily by the increase in NOXA.
source: In any case, these findings indicate that MARCH5 is not altered in response to erlotinib, and that its increased degradation of MCL1 is driven primarily by the increase in NOXA.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experiments examining MARCH5 localization and activity.

claim: Four-hour treatment with actinonin decreased MCL1 in LNCaP cells and increased NOXA.
source: Four-hour treatment with actinonin decreased MCL1 in LNCaP cells (Figure 5A). However, it also increased NOXA, suggesting that it may be acting similarly to tyrosine kinase inhibitors through an ISR, rather than by directly through MARCH5.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5A.

claim: Gamitrinib-TPP rapidly decreased MCL1 in LNCaP cells and was associated with an increase in NOXA.
source: Consistent with previous data (Karpel-Massler et al., 2017; Ishida et al., 2017), gamitrinib-TPP rapidly decreased MCL1 in LNCaP cells, and this was also associated with an increase in NOXA (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5B and citations.

claim: Treatment with CPI-613 decreased MCL1 and increased NOXA.
source: Similar to actinonin and gamitrinib-TPP, treatment with CPI-613 decreased MCL1 and also increased NOXA (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5C.

claim: Each of the mitochondria-targeted agents (actinonin, gamitrinib-TPP, CPI-613) increased ATF4.
source: Significantly, each of these mitochondria-targeted agents increased ATF4 (Figure 5C), indicating an ISR mechanism for increasing NOXA.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5C.

claim: Treatment with ISRIB impaired the upregulation of ATF4 and NOXA, and the reduction of MCL1, by each of the mitochondria-targeted agents.
source: Consistent with this finding, and with a previous report on gamitrinib-TPP (Karpel-Massler et al., 2017), treatment with ISRIB impaired the upregulation of ATF4 and NOXA, and the reduction of MCL1, by each of these mitochondria-targeted agents (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5C and a citation.

claim: Depleting NOXA with siRNA prevented the decrease in MCL1 in response to actinonin, gamitrinib-TPP, and CPI-613.
source: Moreover, depleting NOXA with siRNA prevented the decrease in MCL1 in response to each of these agents (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5D.

claim: The increased MCL1 degradation in response to mitochondria-targeted agents was being driven by increased NOXA downstream of an ISR.
source: Together these findings indicated that the increased MCL1 degradation in response to these agents was being driven by increased NOXA downstream of an ISR.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experiments with ISRIB and NOXA depletion.

claim: The decrease in MCL1 by mitochondria-targeted agents was proteasome-dependent and was not associated with an increase in p53.
source: As further evidence for this conclusion, we found that the decrease in MCL1 by these mitochondria-targeted agents was proteasome-dependent, and was not associated with an increase in p53 (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Depleting MARCH5 markedly increased MCL1 and prevented the MCL1 loss in response to erlotinib and actinonin.
source: Depleting MARCH5 markedly increased MCL1 and prevented the MCL1 loss in response to erlotinib and actinonin, although the effects of gamitrinib-TPP and CPI-613 were only partially suppressed, suggesting other ubiquitin ligases may contribute to this MCL1 degradation and partially compensate for the loss of MARCH5 (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5G.

claim: Depletion of HUWE1 partially impaired the effects of CPI-613 on MCL1.
source: Indeed, depletion of HUWE1 (which more modestly increased MCL1) partially impaired the effects of CPI-613 (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5H.

claim: MCL1 degradation by actinonin in combination with BCLXL/BCL2 inhibition by ABT-263 caused dramatic apoptosis in LNCaP cells.
source: Finally, as expected and consistent with a previous study of gamitrinib-TPP (Karpel-Massler et al., 2017), MCL1 degradation by actinonin in combination with BCLXL/BCL2 inhibition by ABT-263 caused dramatic apoptosis in LNCaP cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and a citation.

claim: Mitochondrial stress, similarly to kinase inhibitors, increases MCL1 degradation primarily through ISR-mediated activation and NOXA-dependent MARCH5-mediated ubiquitylation.
source: Overall, these results indicate that mitochondrial stress, similarly to kinase inhibitors, increases MCL1 degradation primarily through ISR-mediated activation and NOXA-dependent MARCH5-mediated ubiquitylation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experiments with mitochondria-targeted agents.

claim: The MCL1 gene is frequently amplified in multiple cancers, occurring in approximately 10% in the largest reported PCa dataset.
source: Consistent with its antiapoptotic and hence oncogenic function, the MCL1 gene is frequently amplified in multiple cancers (~10% in the largest reported PCa dataset) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by genomic data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Deep deletions of MARCH5 were identified in up to approximately 5% of PCa across a series of data sets.
source: Deep deletions of MARCH5 were identified in up to ~5% of PCa across a series of data sets (Figure 6B), and MARCH5 deletions (either shallow or deep deletion) are associated with shorter progression free survival (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by genomic data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: MARCH5 deletions (either shallow or deep deletion) are associated with shorter progression free survival.
source: Deep deletions of MARCH5 were identified in up to ~5% of PCa across a series of data sets (Figure 6B), and MARCH5 deletions (either shallow or deep deletion) are associated with shorter progression free survival (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: HUWE1 loss was very rare in prostate cancer.
source: In contrast, HUWE1 loss was very rare (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by genomic data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: MARCH5 loss appears to be most common in PCa compared to other cancers.
source: Interestingly, assessing genomic alterations across cancers, MARCH5 loss appears to be most common in PCa (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by genomic data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: MARCH5 loss may reflect its genomic location adjacent to PTEN at 10q23, and hence co-deletion with PTEN.
source: Significantly, this may reflect its genomic location adjacent to PTEN at 10q23, and hence co-deletion with PTEN.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative explanation for the frequency of MARCH5 loss in PCa.

claim: In the TCGA primary PCa dataset, all cases with deep deletion of MARCH5 also have PTEN deletion.
source: Indeed, in the TCGA primary PCa dataset, all cases with deep deletion of MARCH5 also have PTEN deletion (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by genomic data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: MARCH5 deletion appears to be occurring independently of PTEN loss in a subset of metastatic PCa.
source: In contrast, MARCH5 deletion appears to be occurring independently of PTEN loss in a subset of metastatic PCa.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an observation from the genomic data.

claim: MCL1 amplification and MARCH5 loss generally occur in distinct tumors.
source: MCL1 amplification and MARCH5 loss generally occur in distinct tumors, although their mutual exclusivity is not statistically significant (Figure 6F; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by genomic data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Oncogenic alterations in the genes encoding NOXA (PMAIP1) and BIM (BCL2L11) are rare relative to MARCH5 and MCL1.
source: Relative to MARCH5 and MCL1, oncogenic alterations in the genes encoding NOXA (PMAIP1) and BIM (BCL2L11) are rare (Figure 6F; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by genomic data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Shallow deletions of MARCH5 appear to be relatively common in PCa, with a higher frequency in metastatic castration-resistant PCa versus primary PCa.
source: Finally, shallow deletions of MARCH5, suggesting single copy losses, appear to be relatively common in PCa, with a higher frequency in metastatic castration-resistant PCa versus primary PCa (Figure 6G,H; Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by genomic data shown in Figure 6G,H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: The genomic data support a tumor suppressor function for MARCH5, which may be related to its negative regulation of MCL1.
source: Together these results support a tumor suppressor function for MARCH5, which may be related to its negative regulation of MCL1.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the genomic data showing MARCH5 deletions in tumors.

claim: S63845 at 1 μM both stabilized MCL1 and decreased NOXA and BIM in MARCH5 knockout cells.
source: S63845 at the lowest concentration examined (1 μM) both stabilized MCL1 and decreased NOXA and BIM, consistent with S63845 binding to MCL1 and displacing NOXA and BIM, and with their subsequent increased degradation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 7A.

claim: Despite substantial displacement of NOXA and BIM from MCL1 by S63845, the increase in apoptosis was only observed at the highest concentration of drug (20 μM).
source: Surprisingly, despite the apparent substantial displacement of NOXA and BIM from MCL1, the increase in apoptosis (as assessed by cleaved caspase 3, CC3, and cleaved PARP, cPARP) was only observed at the highest concentration of drug (20 μM).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 7A.

claim: AZD5991 showed identical results to S63845 in MARCH5 knockout cells.
source: Identical results were obtained with a second MCL1 antagonist (AZD5991) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 7B.

claim: Cells stably overexpressing ectopic MCL1 had marked increases in NOXA and BIM, which were decreased in response to 1 μM S63845 or AZD5991, but apoptotic responses required high drug concentrations.
source: We also examined cells stably overexpressing ectopic MCL1. These cells similarly had marked increases in NOXA and BIM, which were decreased in response to 1 μM S63845 (Figure 7C) or AZD5991 (Figure 7D), but apoptotic responses again required high drug concentrations.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 7C and 7D.

claim: MCL1 was binding increased levels of BAK, NOXA, and BIM in MARCH5 knockout and MCL1 overexpressing cells.
source: Indeed, we confirmed that MCL1 was binding increased levels of these proteins in MARCH5 knockout and MCL1 overexpressing cells, and that MCL1 antagonists could induce apoptosis in the MARCH5 knockout and MCL1 overexpressing cells, but not the control cells.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 7E.

claim: BAK was not increased in the MARCH5 knockout cells.
source: In support of this latter mechanism, we found that BAK was not increased in the MARCH5 knockout cells (Figure 7F), which may allow the high levels of MCL1 to effectively buffer BAK despite treatment with S63845 or AZD5991.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 7F.

claim: BAX protein expression was decreased in the MARCH5 knockout cells.
source: In contrast to BAK, in the unactivated state BAX is localized primarily in the cytoplasm and may be buffered mostly by BCLXL and BCL2. Significantly, BAX protein expression was decreased in the MARCH5 knockout cells (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 7F.

claim: ABT-263 treatment caused a marked apoptotic response specifically in the MARCH5 knockout cells.
source: Therefore, we assessed responses to the BCL2/BCLXL antagonist ABT-263 (navitoclax). Significantly, ABT-263 treatment caused a marked apoptotic response specifically in the MARCH5 knockout cells (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 7G.

claim: The addition of S63845 only minimally enhanced apoptosis in the ABT-263 treated MARCH5 knockout cells.
source: As we reported previously (Arai et al., 2018), ABT-263 could induce apoptosis in control parental cells in combination with S63845, but the addition of S63845 only minimally enhanced apoptosis in the ABT-263 treated MARCH5 knockout cells (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 7H and a citation.

claim: The BCL2-specific antagonist ABT-199 (venetoclax) was not effective in MARCH5 knockout cells, indicating that the efficacy of ABT-263 is due to BCLXL inhibition.
source: The BCL2-specific antagonist ABT-199 (venetoclax) was not effective, indicating that the efficacy of ABT-263 is due to BCLXL inhibition (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 7I.

claim: The gene that was most co-dependent with MARCH5 in the Avana CRISPR screen dataset was MCL1.
source: Interestingly, the gene that was most co-dependent with MARCH5 was MCL1 (Figure 7J,K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 7J,K.

claim: The gene most co-dependent with MCL1 in the Avana CRISPR screen dataset was MARCH5.
source: Conversely, the gene most co-dependent with MCL1 was MARCH5.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 7J,K.

claim: This strong co-dependency between MARCH5 and MCL1 was also observed in screens with another CRISPR library.
source: This strong co-dependency was also observed in screens with another CRISPR library (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B,C.

claim: MARCH5, while acting as a ubiquitin ligase for NOXA-liganded MCL1, may also have a distinct function in conjunction with MCL1 to suppress mitochondrial membrane permeabilization by BAX.
source: Based on these results and our data, we suggest that MARCH5, while acting as a ubiquitin ligase for NOXA-liganded MCL1, may also have a distinct function in conjunction with MCL1 to suppress mitochondrial membrane permeabilization by BAX.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative interpretation of the co-dependency data and experimental findings.

claim: NOXA binding can increase the degradation of MCL1.
source: In this study we initially found that erlotinib treatment rapidly increased expression of NOXA, and that the increased MCL1 degradation was NOXA-dependent. We subsequently found that the increase in NOXA was driven by ISR activation, with subsequent increase in ATF4 protein and NOXA transcription. Previous studies have shown that NOXA binding can increase the degradation of MCL1 (39), and have implicated the ubiquitin ligases HUWE1 or PARKIN in this degradation (Gomez-Bougie et al., 2011; Zhong et al., 2005; Warr et al., 2005; Carroll et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The physiological significance of MARCH5 as a tumor suppressor gene through regulation of MCL1 is supported by its genomic loss in a subset of cancers.
source: The physiological significance of MARCH5 as a tumor suppressor gene through regulation of MCL1 is further supported by its genomic loss in a subset of cancers.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the genomic data showing MARCH5 deletions.

claim: MARCH5 depleted cells have increased sensitivity to MCL1 antagonists at high concentrations that may have off-target effects.
source: Importantly, MARCH5 depleted cells, which have increased levels of both MCL1 and NOXA, have increased sensitivity to MCL1 antagonists (although at high concentrations that may have off-target effects) and to the BH3 mimetic drug navitoclax (due to targeting BCLXL), suggesting therapeutic approaches for MARCH5-deficient tumors.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experimental data showing responses to MCL1 and BCLXL inhibitors.

claim: ATF4 has been reported to directly upregulate the PMAIP1 gene (encoding NOXA).
source: However, ATF4 has been reported to directly upregulate the PMAIP1 gene (encoding NOXA) (Armstrong et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2009), which would be consistent with the rapid time course of NOXA induction that correlated with increased ATF4.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NOXA binding to MCL1 appears to stabilize a conformation that can drive its interaction with ubiquitin ligases including HUWE1 and MARCH5.
source: NOXA binding to MCL1 appears to stabilize a conformation that can drive its interaction with ubiquitin ligases including HUWE1 and, as shown in this study, with MARCH5 (Gomez-Bougie et al., 2011; Guikema et al., 2017; Song et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations to prior literature and the current study.

claim: MARCH5 is the major ubiquitin ligase mediating NOXA-induced MCL1 degradation.
source: Indeed, the finding that MARCH5 depletion prevented the degradation of MCL1 in response to NOXA induction indicates that MARCH5 is the major ubiquitin ligase mediating NOXA-induced MCL1 degradation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the MARCH5 depletion experiments.

claim: MARCH5 plays a substantial role in regulating MCL1 under basal conditions, although this may still be NOXA-dependent and could reflect constitutive levels of stress in tumor cells.
source: We further found that MARCH5 depletion increased MCL1 in multiple cell lines, indicating that MARCH5 plays a substantial role in regulating MCL1 under basal conditions, although this may still be NOXA-dependent and could reflect constitutive levels of stress in tumor cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the MARCH5 depletion experiments and includes speculation about the mechanism.

claim: A very recent study found that MARCH5 is a major mediator of MCL1 and NOXA degradation in response to taxane-mediated mitotic arrest.
source: Finally, a very recent study found that MARCH5 is a major mediator of MCL1 and NOXA degradation in response to taxane-mediated mitotic arrest (Haschka et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a recent finding from another study and supported by a citation.

claim: All three mitochondria-targeted agents examined (actinonin, gamitrinib-TPP, and CPI-613) caused a MARCH5-dependent increase in MCL1 degradation associated with a stress response, with increased ATF4 and NOXA.
source: Indeed, we found that all three agents examined (actinonin, gamitrinib-TPP, and CPI-613) caused a MARCH5-dependent increase in MCL1 degradation. However, this did not appear to reflect a direct effect on MARCH5. It was instead associated with a stress response, with increased ATF4 and NOXA, similarly to the response to kinase inhibitors.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the experiments with mitochondria-targeted agents.

claim: While the apparent release of BIM and NOXA from MCL1 by S63845 or AZD5991 and their subsequent degradation were observed at relatively low concentrations, the induction of apoptosis required approximately 20 μM of these drugs.
source: However, while the apparent release of BIM and NOXA from MCL1 and their subsequent degradation were observed at relatively low concentrations of S63845 or AZD5991, the induction of apoptosis required ~20 μM of these drugs.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the dose-response experiments with MCL1 antagonists.

claim: The requirement for higher drug levels of MCL1 antagonists may reflect the very high levels of MCL1 and its subsequent persistent engagement of BAK, despite treatment with MCL1 antagonists.
source: This requirement for higher drug levels may reflect the very high levels of MCL1 and its subsequent persistent engagement of BAK, despite treatment with MCL1 antagonists.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative explanation for the high drug concentrations required for apoptosis.

claim: A previous study found that MARCH5 depletion could sensitize to ABT-263, and suggested it may be due to high levels of NOXA that are antagonizing the antiapoptotic functions of MCL1.
source: A previous study similarly found that MARCH5 depletion could sensitize to ABT-263, and suggested it may be due to high levels of NOXA that are antagonizing the antiapoptotic functions of MCL1 (Subramanian et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a previous study and supported by a citation.

claim: The available MCL1 antagonists are all noncovalent and stabilize MCL1, which may limit their ability to abrogate MCL1 interaction with BAK.
source: Importantly, the available MCL1 antagonists are all noncovalent and stabilize MCL1, which may limit their ability to abrogate MCL1 interaction with BAK.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of current MCL1 antagonists.

claim: Antagonists that drive MCL1 degradation, possibly by mimicking the NOXA BH3 domain, might be more potent and effective than current MCL1 antagonists.
source: Therefore, it is possible that antagonists that drive MCL1 degradation, possibly by mimicking the NOXA BH3 domain, might be more potent and effective.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative suggestion for future drug development.

claim: Approaches that selectively cause robust ISR activation in tumor cells, with increased NOXA and MCL1 degradation, may create an exploitable therapeutic window for BCLXL antagonists.
source: Finally, approaches that selectively cause robust ISR activation in tumor cells, with increased NOXA and MCL1 degradation, may create an exploitable therapeutic window for BCLXL antagonists.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative therapeutic strategy based on the study findings.
